 ABSTRACT
Introduction Side-to-side strength differences are often used in return to sport (RTS) decision
making following hamstring injury. In football (soccer), there is little consensus, and a side-to-
side difference of <10% is often suggested as a criterion. To date, no study has determined
whether differences exist when comparing the strength of the injured limb at RTS to the pre-
 D
injury level. Purpose The aim of this study was to compare the isokinetic strength at RTS to pre-
injury strength in the injured limb, and to investigate the side-to-side differences at RTS.
 EP
Methods This study was based on a pooled group of patients participating in two single-site
randomized controlled trials. All eligible professional male soccer players who suffered an MRI-
positive hamstring injury were included. The isokinetic strength of the injured limb at RTS was
 TE
compared to pre-injury screening tests, and the side-to-side difference was determined at both
time points. Results In total, 41 hamstring injuries were included in the analyses. Side-to-side
differences in isokinetic strength at RTS were similar to pre-injury levels. At RTS, the average
strength of the injured limb was >95% compared to pre-injury strength. Overall, 63.4% of the
 C
players had a >10% negative strength difference (i.e. the injured limb being weaker) and 57.9%
of the players had a >10% positive strength difference (i.e. the injured limb being stronger) in at
 C
least one of the five isokinetic variables. Conclusion The distribution of isokinetic strength
differences when comparing strength at RTS to pre-injury measures were similar, urging clinical
A
caution when interpreting these results. Small changes in isokinetic strength of the injured limb
at RTS compared to pre-injury strength suggest that isokinetic cut-off values are not useful to
guide restoration of strength as a criterion for RTS after hamstring injury. Keywords hamstring
injuries; return to sport; criteria; isokinetic; rehabilitation
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 INTRODUCTION
Hamstring injuries are common in sports that involve high speed running such as football
(soccer), American football, Australian football, rugby and sprinting.(1,2) In elite soccer, muscle
injuries represent 18% to 37% of all time-loss injuries,(3–5) and hamstring muscle injuries have
become the most common injury reported.(4) When faced with return to sport (RTS) decisions
 D
following hamstring injury, clinicians, technical staff, and players engage in a type of risk-
benefit analysis.(6) The StARRT framework(7), adapted from the original Creighton model,(8)
 EP
suggests the assessment of health and activity risk, and then an assessment of risk tolerance, to
determine RTS readiness. A recent systematic review of RTS after hamstring injuries
demonstrated that only half of the studies included provide some definition of readiness for RTS,
 TE
with a wide variety of non-validated criteria used to support the decision.(9) Muscle strength, in
particular eccentric hamstring strength, is considered an important criterion when determining
whether a player is ready to RTS after hamstring injury.(10–12) However, in a worldwide Delphi
study conducted to address discrepancies related to RTS criteria after hamstring injuries in
 C
soccer,(13) no consensus was reached to include “similar eccentric strength” as a criterion, with
the expert panel divided. The value of muscle strength tests is unclear.
 C
In elite sports, isokinetic dynamometry tests are widely used as criteria for RTS and during
athlete screening (periodic or pre-participation health evaluations), where strength is typically
A
compared between the injured and uninjured limb. Isokinetic strength is one of the top three
screening tests used at elite level in soccer,(14) even though evidence for this practice is
lacking.(15) Although typically not available in general practice, the addition of isokinetic
testing as a RTS criterion has been suggested,(16) however, it remains unclear if this would
actually lead to more timely RTS and lower re-injury rates. Furthermore, it is often
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 recommended that the strength of the injured muscle is comparable to pre-injury levels, or at
least approximating the strength of the uninjured limb.(7) Although no uniform recommendation
exists, 10% is often considered a benchmark for the injured muscle when compared to the
contralateral uninjured side.(10,11,13)
A previous study found isokinetic testing as a RTS criterion after hamstring injury suspect,
 D
reporting that 67% of the players with a side-to-side deficit of >10% in at least one isokinetic
measure at RTS.(17) The main limitation of this and other similar studies is the assumption that
 EP
the uninjured side represents the pre-injury (“healthy”) strength status of the injured leg. As
hamstring strength might be considered a risk factor for hamstring injury,(15,18) it is possible
that the observed side-to-side difference was already present preceding the hamstring injury, or
 TE
perhaps the uninjured limb was strengthened during rehabilitation. However, there are no studies
comparing results from pre-injury screening data to strength at RTS. Also, the minimal
detectable change (the smallest amount of change required to distinguish a true performance
difference from variability due to measurement error) in isokinetic tests has been reported as
 C
high as 20.6% and 24.0% for quadriceps and hamstrings muscles, respectively.(19) Therefore,
the ability to interpret a difference in hamstring strength is also limited by test accuracy.
 C
Thus, the purpose of this study was to determine whether professional soccer players who had
suffered MRI-positive acute hamstring injuries displayed the same level of strength as measured
A
during pre-season baseline testing. We aimed to compare isokinetic strength of the injured limb
at RTS to pre-injury strength measures, and to assess the side-to-side differences at RTS.
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 METHODS
This study was based on a pooled group of patients participating in two single-site randomized
controlled trials (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT01812564 and NCT02104258). The first trial
(the growth factor study) investigated the effect of platelet-rich plasma injections and has been
completed, with 90 participants included between 2009 and 2013.(20) The second trial (the
 D
Aspetar hamstring rehabilitation study) was initiated in 2014, investigating the effect of two
rehabilitation protocols with different emphasis on eccentric (lengthening) exercises on time to
 EP
RTS and rate of re-injury. This trial is ongoing, and at the time of analysis (August 2018), 85 out
of 90 participants had been randomized and completed their treatment.
Eligibility criteria
 TE
Data were collected between November 2009 and July 2018 from players meeting the eligibility
criteria in the respective rehabilitation trials (table 1). For the purpose of the current study,
professional soccer players competing in Qatar were eligible. Each player underwent an annual
periodic health evaluation (commonly referred to as screening) at the Aspetar Orthopaedic and
 C
Sports Medicine Hospital in Doha, Qatar. As part of the musculoskeletal component of the
periodic health evaluation, all players received a comprehensive musculoskeletal test battery
 C
aimed at identifying potential biomechanical and anatomic risk factors for lower extremity
injuries at the rehabilitation department of Aspetar.(21) Players that had isokinetic testing
A
performed during their annual periodic health evaluation and suffered a subsequent hamstring
injury that was included in either of the two rehabilitation trials, were included in the current
study. All players signed a consent form ahead of inclusion. Ethical approvals were obtained
from the Institutional Review Board, Anti-doping Laboratory, Qatar (IRB F2013000003 and IRB
F2013000009).
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 Diagnosis of an acute hamstring injury was performed by a sports medicine physician and
included a comprehensive patient history, physical examination, and confirmatory MRI. In both
trials, athletes were included if a positive clinical examination was confirmed by a positive MRI
diagnosis. (Note that the described inclusion criteria between the two trials differ slightly as
presented in table 1.) Radiological grading of the injuries was performed by the same radiologist
using the most commonly accepted grading system defining four grades: grade 0 with no
 D
pathological findings, grade 1 with muscle oedema only but without tissue damage, grade 2 as
partial muscle tear and grade 3 with a complete muscle tear.(22) Players with negative MRI
 EP
results, even if they had a positive history and physical signs of hamstring injury (e.g. acute
mechanism of onset, palpable tenderness, and localized pain on resisted hamstring contraction),
were excluded.
Isokinetic testing
 TE
Isokinetic strength testing (System 3, Biodex, New York, USA) was performed on three separate
occasions: 1) during the annual periodic health evaluation (both limbs) pre-injury, 2) during the
 C
initial examination within seven days post-injury (contralateral uninjured limb only), and 3) prior
to the final RTS assessment (both limbs).
 C
Prior to isokinetic testing, the athletes were instructed as to the nature and purpose of the
isokinetic testing. They performed a standardized warm-up procedure comprising five minutes
A
on a stationary exercise bike (Technogym, Italy) at a resistance (in W) equivalent to 1.5 times
their bodyweight (in kg) at their chosen cadence (typically this was approximately 85 rpm). Prior
to each isokinetic test, the athlete was instructed as to the mode of testing, and given a minimum
of three practice repetitions, and testing was not started unless the athlete thought they were
ready to do so. For the periodic health evaluation, the order (i.e. left, right) was randomized, and
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 this was maintained for all the different modes and speeds for that athlete. At discharge, the
uninjured limb was tested first, followed by the injured limb. During testing, vigorous verbal
encouragement was provided.
Testing comprised three modes and speeds. First, the players were tested over five repetitions of
concentric knee flexion and extension at 60°/s, followed by 10 repetitions of concentric knee
 D
flexion and extension at 300°/s. These test modes measured the concentric strength of the
“quadriceps” (knee extension) and “hamstring” (knee flexion) muscles. Finally, players
 EP
performed five repetitions of eccentric knee extension at 60°/s which measured the eccentric
strength of the knee flexors (principally the “hamstring” muscles). The reliability of the
isokinetic tests has been described previously.(19)
 TE
Standardized rehabilitation protocols
The participants in both randomized control trials completed comparable standardized criteria-
based rehabilitation protocols. The protocols included range of motion exercises, progressive
strengthening exercises and an incremental, progressive return to running program. The
 C
rehabilitation was performed at one location, supervised by one of six sports physical therapists
with 7–25 years of experience treating athletes. The (treating) physiotherapist was blinded to the
 C
MRI findings. In both trials functional, criteria-based progressions (as opposed to time-based
progressions) were utilized for the six-stage rehabilitation protocols.(17,23) The rehabilitation
A
protocol for the first study has been published,(17) and the structure of the two different
protocols used in the
(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fzex_zG1JtA;
 second trial is freely available online:
http://www.aspetar.com/AspetarFILEUPLOAD/UploadCenter/636209313253275549_Aspetar%
20Hamstring%20Protocol.pdf )
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 Soccer-specific training
After successfully finishing the first three stages of the rehabilitation protocol, the final stages of
soccer-specific training were supervised by a sports rehabilitator with more than 10 years of
experience in professional soccer. The protocol consisted of three stages (typically completed in
three days) and progression of volume and intensity of direction changes, sprints, jumps, passes,
shooting, interval running, one-on-one attacking and defending drills. The training was designed
 D
to mimic muscle fatigue and competitiveness during soccer training and game situations.
Successful completion of the soccer-specific training was defined as full sports-specific
 EP
functional ability without obvious limitations and/or symptoms.(17)
Return to sport
 TE
The player had to complete the soccer-specific training before the RTS assessment was
performed. The treating sports medicine physician was informed of the physical therapists‟ RTS
assessment findings, which included clinical examinations, as well as any comments from the
sports rehabilitator regarding the on-field sessions. With this information (from the physical
 C
therapist and sports rehabilitator), the sports medicine physician then took a history, performed a
clinical examination, and then decided on the athlete‟s readiness to RTS. RTS was defined as the
 C
number of days between initial injury and return to full unrestricted training and/or match
play.(17) Acute hamstring strain injuries at the same site that occurred within 2 months from
A
RTS, were classified as re-injuries.(4,24)
Statistical analyses
All statistical analyses were performed with Excel 2016 (Microsoft, Redmond, USA) and SPSS
software (V.20.0; SPSS, Chicago, Illinois, USA). Continuous variables were expressed as mean
with standard deviation (SD). We analyzed differences in binomial data between groups with an
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 unpaired t test. Significance was assumed if the p value was less than 0.05. The percentage was
calculated of players with 5%, 10%, 15%, 20% and 25% isokinetic strength difference when
comparing 1) the contralateral limbs pre-injury, 2) the contralateral limbs at RTS, and 3) the
ipsilateral limb pre-injury to RTS.
RESULTS
 D
The inclusion of players into the study is outlined in figure 1. In total, 41 soccer players (age 25
± 4 yrs, height 175 ± 6 cm, body mass 71 ± 7 kg, body mass index 23 ± 2 kg/m2) were included.
 EP
There was no significant difference in any of these measures between the 72 excluded players
(age 24 ± 5 yrs, height 177 ± 6 cm, weight 73 ± 9 kg, body mass index [BMI] 23 ± 2 kg/m2) and
the 41 players included (p >0.05).
 TE
Of the 41 injuries, 21 were classified as grade I injuries and 20 as grade II, with 73.1% located in
the biceps femoris long head, 22.0% in the semimembranosus, and 4.9% in the semitendinosus.
The injured players included six forwards, 17 midfielders, 17 defenders, and one goalkeeper. The
 C
players included in this analysis took on average 25.3 ± 8.9 days to RTS. One player suffered a
re-injury from the completed trial.
 C
The isokinetic strength of the players pre-injury during the periodic health evaluation (both
limbs), post-injury at initial assessment (uninjured limb only), and at RTS (both limbs) is
A
presented in figure 2, demonstrating only small changes in strength between the measurements.
Quadriceps and hamstrings concentric strength at 60°/s demonstrated statistically significant
differences of 4.9% and 5.3% respectively when comparing the injured limb at RTS to pre-injury
(table 2).
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 At RTS, the average strength of the injured limbs was >95% normalized to the pre-injury
strength for all measurements (table 2). The side-to-side differences in isokinetic strength are
presented as percentages for isokinetic strength pre-injury (panel A) and at RTS (panel B). The
same cut-offs are used when comparing the change in strength at RTS to pre-injury in the injured
limb (panel C); figure 3 demonstrating a negative difference (i.e. the injured leg was weaker) and
figure 4 a positive difference (i.e. the injured leg was stronger). The greatest difference (non-
 D
significant with large CIs) was found for the cut-offs of >20% when comparing panel C to panels
A and B (figure 3).
 EP
Overall, 63.4% of the players had a >10% negative side-to-side strength difference (i.e. injured
limb being weaker) and 57.9% of the players had a >10% positive strength difference (i.e.
 TE
injured limb being stronger) in at least one of the five isokinetic variables (figures 3 and 4).
DISCUSSION
In this series of 41 professional soccer players with an MRI-confirmed hamstring injury, novel
analyses, comparing isokinetic strength of the injured limb at RTS to pre-injury strength
 C
measures, are presented, as well as between-limb comparisons. The present results suggest that a
10% difference (positive or negative) is present in a large proportion of players at RTS following
 C
hamstring injury, and the distribution of isokinetic strength variables in the injured limb at RTS
are similar to pre-injury strength measures. Additionally, the side-to-side strength differences
A
are similar at RTS when compared to pre-injury strength differences.
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 Return to sport decision making after hamstring injury
Only one previous study has investigated isokinetic strength at RTS, suggesting that restoration
of isokinetic strength (compared to the uninjured limb) does not seem to be required for the
successful completion of a criteria based rehabilitation program.(17) However, this comparison
was made between limbs, comparing the injured to the uninjured side. The present study is the
first to compare RTS strength to pre-injury strength in the same limb.
 D
Making RTS decisions following hamstring injuries is challenging. Different criteria have been
 EP
suggested, but there is a lack of validated criteria and poor consensus on which measurements
are useful to determine readiness to RTS.(9) Although evidence to support a specific
 TE
recommendation is lacking, a cut-off of 10% compared to the uninjured side continues to be
prevalent in research studies and clinical practice.(13) However, the present results suggest that a
10% difference (positive or negative) is present in a large proportion of players at RTS following
hamstring injury and is even observed in a similar proportion of players pre-injury.
Regardless of statistical significance, the small changes in the isokinetic measures and large
 C
confidence intervals suggest that it would be clinically meaningless to impose a specific cut-off
value as a criterion for RTS (figure 2). Furthermore, it is clear from figure 3C that a large
 C
percentage of players displayed strength changes in the injured limb at RTS compared to pre-
injury strength for all the isokinetic variables. The side-to-side differences observed pre-injury
A
and at RTS (figure 3A and 3B) are similar to the change in the injured limb (figure 3C), apart
from a greater percentage of players demonstrating a >20% difference at RTS. It remains
difficult to determine which isokinetic strength cut-offs are useful to determine when players are
ready for RTS, or indeed, which players are at greater risk of re-injury.
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 Risk of re-injury
Risk of re-injury is considered a potential decision modifier,(7) with recurrent injuries typically
reported to occur early after RTS.(25–28) Isokinetic strength differences with specific cut-offs
are thought to identify players at greater risk of re-injury, and therefore promoted as a criterion
not only in RTS,(29) but also when used to determine progression during a criteria-based
 D
rehabilitation program.(12) As the second trial from which we included players is still ongoing,
we were unable to investigate re-injury data, and only one of the players from the completed trial
 EP
suffered a re-injury within the first two months.
However, a previous investigation in the same cohort as this present study (53.7% of the players
 TE
in the current study were also included in the previous analysis) reported no differences in
isokinetic strength at RTS between those players who experienced hamstring re-injury, and those
who did not.(17) A recent randomized trial among recreational athletes, comparing early and
delayed rehabilitation, also found no difference in isokinetic strength at RTS, reporting just one
re-injury for the entire cohort.(30) These findings(17,30) suggest that isokinetic strength may not
 C
need to be fully restored to limit re-injury risk if a criteria-based rehabilitation program is
completed successfully.
 C
Isokinetic strength differences
A
Isokinetic side-to-side strength differences at RTS are commonly presented as deficits.(11,17,29)
This may reflect a bias in our view of strength profiles, as strength is preferentially reported as
what is “missing”, i.e. the injured leg being weaker. However, as demonstrated in figure 4, a
similarly large proportion of players present with a positive strength difference, i.e. the injured
leg being stronger. Thus, approximately 60% of the players had at least one negative or positive
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 isokinetic hamstring strength difference of more than 10%. Strength differences, whether
positive or negative, seem to be a standard finding for isokinetic dynamometry testing, and so-
called “deficits” should be interpreted with caution.
There were no significant differences in strength of the uninjured limb for any of the isokinetic
modes of testing pre-injury compared to the post-injury tests during the initial assessment (figure
 D
2). Although we observe a slight decrease in strength in the uninjured limb post-injury, the
reason for this is not known. Quadriceps and hamstrings concentric strength at 60°/s
 EP
demonstrated a statistically significant change in the injured limb (table 2) between RTS and pre-
injury strength, but the small absolute differences are well within the minimal detectable change
values for these modes of isokinetic testing.(29) Together with the large confidence intervals,
 TE
these small differences indicate little clinical value in this finding.
Variability
The asymmetries presented may form useful reference data for clinicians. Importantly, these data
should be interpreted in light of the variability within isokinetic testing that has been previously
 C
documented.(29) In figure 3 and 4, where we compare the strength at RTS to pre-injury, as well
as side-to-side differences, the 95% CI includes 50% of the population for any of the varying
 C
cut-points from 5% to 20%.
A
If we consider that the minimal detectable change in peak torque for all these measures is greater
than 20%,(19) it is apparent that the previously suggested 10% cut-point is likely overly
conservative; beyond the capability of the measurement due to a large amount of intra-individual
variability. Recently, we have also shown that isokinetic strength varies by 15% from one pre-
season to the next.(31) If we were to compare the pre-injury and RTS strength, these results
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 would need to be interpreted in light of the substantial variability we might expect within
individual players over time.
It seems that 20% is more likely a reasonable „cut-point‟ for when an isokinetic strength
difference represents a true difference, however, this cut-off requires further investigation as a
potential risk factor. The use of isokinetic testing in isolation is not supported, and can at best
only be considered a component in RTS decision making.(32)
Strengths and limitations
 D
 EP
A major strength of this study is that all tests performed utilized the same isokinetic testing
system with highly experienced assessors, and it was performed in a single clinical setting for
 TE
professional athletes. All players underwent standardized criteria-based rehabilitation protocols,
together with a standardized and comprehensive RTS assessment. The hamstring injuries
included were confirmed with both clinical examinations and positive MRI results. However,
since only grade I and II injuries were included, it remains unknown if our results can be
extrapolated to MRI negative or grade III (complete avulsions) hamstring injuries.
 C
The isokinetic dynamometry strength testing was performed at the end of the final soccer
 C
specific training session as part of the RTS assessment. Therefore, players may have been
somewhat fatigued at the time of testing, and it is not known whether this may have influenced
A
the results. Although the isokinetic test results were not used as a set criterion in the RTS
decision, the sports medicine physician were not blinded to the results. Since we could not
control the weighting and influence of every bit of information used in the process, we cannot be
sure how the isokinetic results, or indeed a number of other factors, may have influenced the
RTS decision.
Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 An important limitation in this study is incomplete re-injury data. Although only one re-injury
was registered from the completed trial, we do not know the re-injury rate in the second trial.
This study was performed in a multinational, multi-language setting, and while every effort was
made to guarantee that players comprehended the test procedure and directions, it is possible that
some players did not fully understand the instructions. We also acknowledge the homogeneity of
 D
our study population of professional male soccer players, which limits the generalization of these
findings to other sports, age groups or female players.
Clinical implications
 EP
The use of isokinetic strength testing in isolation as a criterion for RTS is not supported by these
 TE
data. Importantly, side-to-side isokinetic strength differences are common at RTS, and when
compared to pre-injury strength. The injured limb presents with similar strength differences
when comparing strength at RTS to pre-injury measures, and in a large proportion of players it
might favor the injured limb. The previous accepted cut-off of 10% is inappropriate, as side-to-
side strength differences of 5-20% are commonly found, both at RTS and pre-injury.
CONCLUSION C
 C
The distribution of positive and negative isokinetic strength differences when comparing strength
at RTS to pre-injury measures were similar, urging clinical caution when interpreting these
A
results. Small changes in isokinetic strength of the injured limb at RTS compared to pre-injury
strength suggest that isokinetic cut-off values are not useful to guide restoration of strength as a
criterion for RTS after hamstring injury.

{
 "id": "Q52",
 "sourceFile": "Single nucleotide polymorphisms and tendon-ligament injuries in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms and Tendon/Ligament Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Healthy Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review of 31 studies (1,687 injured and 2,227 control athletes) of genetic variants and tendon or ligament injury across several sports, with a meta-analysis of 12 studies covering four variants. Only the VEGFA rs699947 C allele was associated with a lower injury risk (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.98, p = 0.03, I2 = 3.82%), and COL1A1 rs1800012, COL5A1 rs12722 and MMP3 rs679620 showed no significant association.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The VEGFA estimate pools only four studies (408 cases, 395 controls), and most included studies are small candidate-gene designs, so the associations are not causal. Only the allele model was significant; the dominant and recessive models were not (OR 0.72 and 0.75), and the dominant model had I2 of 51.9%, which the conclusions describe as confirmed heterogeneity.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read VEGFA rs699947 as a usable genetic marker for tendon and ligament injury risk, but it is one borderline allele-model result from four studies, with the other genetic models null, and it cannot be used to screen or select athletes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Fukuyama Y, Murakami H, Iemitsu M. Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms and Tendon/Ligament Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Int J Sports Med. 2024.",
  "doi": "10.1055/a-2419-4359",
  "abstract": "The review aimed to identify associations between genetic polymorphisms and tendon and ligament injuries in adolescent and adult athletes of multiple sports. It included 31 articles (1,687 injury cases and 2,227 controls) and identified 144 candidate polymorphisms, and the meta-analysis of 12 articles covered COL1A1 rs1800012, COL5A1 rs12722, MMP3 rs679620 and VEGFA rs699947. Only VEGFA rs699947 was associated with injury, with the C allele linked to a lower risk (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.98).",
  "tldr": "One gene variant (VEGFA rs699947, C allele) was linked to about 20% lower tendon and ligament injury risk in athletes, based on four studies. The other candidate variants showed no clear link, so genetic screening for these injuries is not supported yet.",
  "methods": "Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020, searching PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCO, Cochrane Library and MEDLINE to 7 July 2023 for genetic association studies of tendon or ligament injury in athletes. Study quality was rated with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and pooled odds ratios used DerSimonian and Laird random-effects models.",
  "findings": "Of 144 candidate polymorphisms in 31 studies, four were pooled. For VEGFA rs699947, the C allele versus A allele gave OR 0.80 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.98, p = 0.03, I2 = 3.82%), while the dominant (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.18, I2 = 51.9%) and recessive (OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.12) models were not significant. COL1A1 rs1800012, COL5A1 rs12722 and MMP3 rs679620 showed no significant effect in any genetic model.",
  "limitations": "The VEGFA finding rests on four studies, and few candidate-gene studies met meta-analysis criteria. The mechanisms of several variants are unclear, many studies came from one region so ethnic comparisons are limited, and competitive level, training time and nutrition were not accounted for.",
  "practicalImplications": "Genetic variants are not yet usable to identify athletes at risk of tendon or ligament injury. The VEGFA result needs replication in larger samples before any practical use.",
  "athleteDev": "This review cannot inform athlete development or training choices, since it covers injury association only. Genotype-based selection or program design is not supported by these findings.",
  "rtp": "Cannot guide return to sport: the review compares injured and uninjured athletes and gives no information on rehabilitation, recovery or return timelines."
 }
}

import json
d=json.load(open('drafts/Q52.json'))
p=d['paper']
d['evidenceSummary']='Systematic review of 31 genetic association studies of tendon or ligament injury in athletes across several sports, with a meta-analysis of 12 studies (1,687 injured and 2,227 control athletes) covering four variants. p['abstract']='The review aimed to identify associations between genetic polymorphisms and tendon and ligament injuries in adolescent and adult athletes of multiple sports. It included 31 articles and identified 144 candidate polymorphisms, and the meta-analysis of 12 articles (1,687 injury cases and 2,227 controls) covered COL1A1 rs1800012, COL5A1 rs12722, MMP3 rs679620 and VEGFA rs699947. Only VEGFA rs699947 was associated with injury, with the C allele linked to a lower risk (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.98).'

json.dump(d,open('verified/Q52.json','w'),indent=1,ensure_ascii=False)

61: Abstract
 2
 Abstract
A vegan diet is associated with reduced cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, but protein
deficiencies may be detrimental to skeletal muscle structure and function. The aim of this
study was to compare the vascular and skeletal muscle properties between young, healthy,
recreationally active habitual vegan (VEG) and omnivorous (OMN) men. Sixteen OMN and
nine VEG underwent ultrasound scans to determine brachial artery flow-mediated dilation
(FMD) and carotid artery intima-media thickness (cIMT) and vastus lateralis (VL) muscle
thickness and fascicle pennation angle. Knee extension maximal voluntary isometric
contraction (MVIC) force was assessed on an isokinetic dynamometer, and 𝑉̇ O2max on a cycle
ergometer and online gas analysis system. A three-day food diary determined habitual dietary
behaviour. Bayesian analyses of independent groups provided ‘moderate’ to ‘very strong’
evidence for lower consumption of absolute (63±21 g/d vs. 98±30 g/d; Bayes Factor
(BF01)=0.140) and relative (0.86±0.29 g/kg/d vs. 1.36±0.52 g/kg/d; BF01=0.259) protein,
absolute saturated fat (15.2±7.9 g vs. 30.3±11.8 g; BF01=0.089) and cholesterol (5.0±6.0 mg
vs. 337.9±232.6 mg; BF01=0.019) in VEG compared to OMN, respectively. Further, there
was ‘anecdotal’ evidence to support no differences in FMD (3.37±3.31% vs. 4.58±5.82%;
BF01=2.591), cIMT (0.51±0.07mm vs. 0.49±0.04mm; BF01=2.510), VL thickness
(26.1±3.7mm vs. 27.8±6.4mm; BF01=2.726), fascicle pennation angle (16.6±4.7° vs.
17.7±3.7°; BF01=2.844), MVIC (627±182 N vs. 551±102 N; BF01=1.656) or 𝑉̇ O2max
(40.8±9.8 ml/kg/min vs. 35.8±5.2 ml/kg/min; BF01=1.218) between VEG and OMN,
respectively. Despite marked differences in habitual nutrient intake, healthy, young vegan
and omnivorous men did not differ regarding vascular and skeletal muscle structure and
function, or cardiovascular fitness.
Key words: diet, skeletal muscle, ultrasonography, endothelium, vascular

function assessed via flow-mediated dilation (FMD) are commonly used surrogate markers of

content.content:
96	brachial artery FMD compared with omnivores (Lin et al., 2001) albeit with a suboptimal
97	measurement approach for FMD (Thijssen et al., 2019). More recently, research has
98	demonstrated lower cIMT in young healthy vegetarian men compared with their omnivorous
99	counterparts (Acosta-Navarro et al., 2017). To our knowledge there is only one study that has
100	investigated the effects of a vegan diet on the vasculature, indicating that microvascular
101	function did not improve following just four weeks compliance to a vegan diet (Rogerson et
102	al., 2018). Consequently, it is unclear whether a habitual vegan diet confers any direct
103	benefits to vascular structure or function.
104	Despite the purported health benefits, there are potential risks of nutrient deficiencies
105	associated with vegan diets. Protein intake, for example, is lower in vegan dieters compared
106	with omnivores, and in some cases less than the minimum recommended daily protein intake
107	(Sobiecki et al., 2016). Protein consumption increases postprandial myofibrillar protein
108	synthesis (MPS) rates (Tipton et al., 1999), subsequently contributing to muscle mass
109	accretion (Hartman et al., 2007). Given that muscle mass is the main determinant of
110	maximum strength (Jones et al., 1989), it is plausible that lower protein consumption in
111	 4
112	 vegan diets could be associated with (smaller and therefore) weaker muscles (Sahni et al.,
113	2015). However, previous studies have demonstrated no differences in upper and lower body
114	one-repetition maximum (1-RM) (Boutros et al., 2020), or knee extensor isokinetic peak
115	torque between young physically active vegan/vegetarian and omnivorous women (Lynch et
116	al., 2016) Nonetheless, as participants were highly trained, it is not clear how training status
117	and the interaction with diet may have impacted these findings. It should also be noted that
118	no prior studies have included assessment of muscle morphology or architecture. Skeletal
119	muscle architecture (including thickness and fascicle pennation angle) are key determinants
120	of the maximum force of a muscle (Aagaard et al., 2001), therefore assessment of muscle
121	architecture in habitual, untrained vegan and omnivorous dieters may confirm existing
122	evidence suggesting similarities in maximal muscle strength.
123	Despite the potential disadvantages of plant-based diets for strength/power performance,
124	evidence suggests no differences exist in maximal power output during an incremental
125	cycling bout between vegans, lacto-ovovegetarians and omnivores (Nebl et al., 2019).
126	Contrarily, there is some evidence that 𝑉̇ O2max is higher in female elite vegetarian vs.
127	omnivore endurance athletes (Lynch et al., 2016). Further, highly physically active (150-200
128	minutes of moderate intensity physical activity/week) vegan females exhibit a greater
129	estimated 𝑉̇ O2max when compared with omnivores (Boutros et al., 2020). However,
130	estimating rather than measuring 𝑉̇ O2max is problematic and both studies used highly trained
131	populations, which limits the application of the study findings. For example, chronic
132	endurance (McPhee et al., 2009) and resistance (Erskine et al., 2011; Erskine et al., 2010)
133	exercise, as well as ageing (Janssen et al., 2000) induce physiological adaptations that will
134	likely confound any measurable effect of diet on vascular or muscle properties.
135	To date, no study has combined ultrasound assessments of vascular structure and function
136	with skeletal muscle architecture, as well as maximal force and measured 𝑉̇ O2max, in habitual
137	 5
138	 vegan and omnivorous dieters. The aim of this study, therefore, was to compare the vascular
139	and skeletal muscle properties between young, healthy, untrained men who were either
140	habitual vegan or omnivorous dieters. We hypothesised that vegan dieters would have higher
141	FMD and 𝑉̇ O2max, but lower cIMT values compared with omnivorous dieters, whereas
142	omnivores would have larger and stronger knee extensor muscles.
143	Methods
144	Twenty-five young, healthy men with no history of resistance or endurance exercise training
145	in the preceding six months were recruited for the current study, which was a single-centre,
146	cross-sectional design. Participant characteristics are shown in Table 1. Further exclusion
147	criteria included smokers, those with a history of lower limb injuries in the six months prior
148	to testing and those engaging in more than two hours per week of structured exercise.
149	Participants were established as vegans or omnivores via a series of questions regarding
150	consumption of meat, fish/seafood, eggs and dairy products such as milk and cheese.
151	Subsequently, vegans were defined as those who consumed no animal products in their diet
152	for at least six months prior to testing, and omnivores were defined as those who consumed
153	animal products (including meat) in their habitual diet. This was then confirmed following
154	completion of a three-day food diary (see below). Sixteen omnivores (OMN) and nine vegans
155	(VEG) provided written informed consent prior to taking part in the study, which was
156	approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Liverpool John Moores University (approval
157	number: U18SPS007) and complied with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical
158	Association, 2013).
159	Experimental design. All participants visited the laboratory on three occasions and were
160	instructed to abstain from alcohol (at least 24 h before each visit) and caffeine consumption
161	the day of each visit. Additionally, the participants underwent an overnight fast and avoided
162	exercise for 24 hours prior to the first visit. During the first visit, a brachial artery FMD and
163	 6
164	 cIMT assessment was conducted by the same trained sonographer for all trials. Following the
165	vascular assessment, participants were familiarised with the protocol for the knee extension
166	maximum voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) assessment in the right leg on the
167	isokinetic dynamometer (IKD), and the 𝑉̇ O2max test on a cycle ergometer, for which they
168	completed the warm-up and first stage only. Participants were then provided with a three-day
169	food diary and received full instructions on how to complete the diary. During visit two,
170	subjects underwent an assessment of vastus lateralis (VL) muscle architecture using
171	ultrasonography and completed a quadriceps MVIC on the IKD. The final visit occurred at
172	least two days following visit two and incorporated a 𝑉̇ O2max test to volitional fatigue on a
173	cycle ergometer.
174	Vascular Assessment. Participants arrived at the laboratory at 08.00 hours. They then lay in
175	the supine position for 20 min before extending their right arm at an approximate 80° angle
176	from the torso. All ultrasound measures were carried out by the same trained sonographer
177	using high-resolution ultrasonography (Acuson, Terason, t3000, Teratec, USA) with a 40 mm
178	wide 10-12 MHz probe.
179	FMD was assessed in the brachial artery in the distal third of the upper arm at an angle of
180	60°. Ultrasound parameters remained constant throughout each assessment, with the probe
181	held in a constant position, to optimize longitudinal two-dimensional B mode images of the
182	near arterial wall. A 1 min baseline measurement of artery diameter was recorded prior to a
183	rapid inflator (AG 101 Hokanson, Bellevue, USA) inflating the forearm cuff to 220 mmHg
184	for a 5 min ischaemic stimulus. The endothelium-mediated vasodilation response to the cuff
185	deflation was then recorded, beginning 30 s prior to deflation, for a period of 3 min,
186	according to previous guidelines (Thijssen et al., 2019). Post-test analysis was performed
187	using custom designed automated edge detection and wall tracking software. B mode images
188	were analysed at ~20 Hz, with a specific region of interest identified and lumen diameter then
189	 7
190	 calculated by averaging the number of pixel columns in each frame. Shear rate (SR) was then
191	calculated as the area under the curve (AUC) up to maximal post-deflation diameter. The
192	test-retest coefficient of variation (CV) for FMD measurements previously performed in our
193	laboratory is 11.7% (Carter et al., 2019), which is within the acceptable limits of 15%
194	(Thijssen et al., 2019).
195	For cIMT assessment, participants remained in the supine position, with the head tilted 90° to

206	diameter over the 6-8 s. The mean cIMT and diameter calculated from the 3 recorded angles
207	is presented. The test-retest CVs for carotid artery wall thickness and diameter measurements

209	VL Muscle Architecture. Participants were seated in an IKD chair (Lido Active, Loredan,

214	VL were determined at 50% of the muscle length to establish the middle of the muscle belly
215	 8
216	 for the assessment. Two sagittal ultrasound images were taken at this site with the probe
217	placed perpendicular to the skin, in line with the muscle fascicles. Depth and frequency were
218	altered to obtain the optimal image, with both deep and superficial aponeuroses and at least
219	three fascicles clearly visible. Subsequently, images were analysed using a computer software
220	package (NIH ImageJ, version 1.39b, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, USA). Muscle
221	thickness was measured using the mean value from three measurements of the distance

226	Knee Extension MVIC. Participants remained seated in the IKD as above. They were securely
227	strapped with inextensible straps around the waist and chest to prevent movement, and the
228	right ankle was strapped to the force transducer (KAP, Bienfait B.V. Haarlem, The
229	Netherlands). Force output was recorded using a data acquisition package (Acqknowledge,
230	Biopac Systems, CA, USA). Ten submaximal contractions were completed as a warm-up
231	with participants increasing their force output each time. Once fully prepared, participants
232	were instructed to perform two MVICs separated by a one-minute rest period. The true
233	MVIC value was determined by a difference of < 5 % between each trial, with trials being
234	repeated if larger differences occurred. Verbal encouragement was provided by researchers
235	and feedback was provided to participants by projecting their MVIC attempts on a screen in
236	front of them in real time. Test-retest CV for the MVIC measurement in this study was 4.5%.
237	𝑉̇ O2max. During the final visit participants completed a 𝑉̇ O2max test to volitional fatigue on a
238	cycle ergometer (Lode Corival, Groningen, Netherlands). Upon arrival at the laboratory
239	participants rested for ten minutes before their resting heart rate was measured (Polar,
240	Kempele, Finland) and their blood lactate measurement (Nova Biomedical, Massachusetts,
241	 9
242	 USA) was taken from a finger prick blood sample. The participant was fitted with a facemask
243	to collect inspired and expired air. The test began with a 3 min warm up cycling at a power
244	output of 50 W, before the first stage started with subjects cycling at 95 W. The power output
245	increased by 35 W every 3 min until volitional fatigue, with heart rate (HR), blood lactate and
246	rate of perceived exertion (RPE via Borg Scale) recorded at the end of each increment.
247	Expired air samples were measured using an online gas analysis system (Cortex, Leipzig,
248	Germany) to determine 𝑉̇ O2 and respiratory exchange ratio (RER). The criteria to determine
249	whether 𝑉̇ O2max had been reached consisted of a HR value within 10 bpm of subjects’ age-
250	predicted HR maximum (220-minus age in years), a blood lactate value > 8.0 mmol.L-1, an
251	RER > 1.15 and if subjects were unable to maintain the optimum cycling cadence of 80 rpm.
252	Final HR, blood lactate, RER and RPE measurements were taken immediately following
253	cessation of the test. Test-retest CV for 𝑉̇ O2max assessment in this study was 5.2%.
254	Dietary Analysis. Participants were provided with a three-day food diary with full
255	instructions to record all food and drink consumed over two weekdays (Thursday and Friday)
256	and one weekend day (Saturday). A three-day food diary was deemed appropriate, as
257	opposed to the seven-day method that has previously been suggested to decrease in validity in

259	and Subar, 2017). Time of consumption and quantity of food were also recorded. Dietary

261	Edition (v5.5), Dublin, Ireland), which produced a full dietary report (including macro and

269	independent groups, comprising a null hypothesis (H0 = there are no differences between

307	Discussion
308	This is the first study to combine ultrasound assessments of vascular and skeletal muscle
309	properties, as well as maximal muscle force and 𝑉̇ O2max, for comparison between healthy,
310	young, untrained habitual vegan and omnivorous men. Importantly, by assessing young,
311	recreationally active but non-resistance/endurance trained individuals, we were able to
312	examine the effect of a vegan diet on the vasculature and musculature independent of training
313	status and ageing. Our novel findings demonstrate that no differences existed in vascular
314	structure and function, or skeletal muscle properties, between habitual vegan and omnivorous
315	 12
316	 dieters despite marked differences in macro- and micronutrient intake. Additionally, vegans
317	and omnivores did not differ regarding cardiorespiratory fitness.
318	Prior research has demonstrated both higher FMD scores and smaller cIMT values in
319	vegetarians compared with omnivores (Acosta-Navarro et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2001).
320	However, in our study, we demonstrate in a young, recreationally active male cohort that
321	there were no differences in vascular structure or function between vegans and omnivores,
322	despite vegans consuming less saturated fat and cholesterol in their diet. One possible
323	explanation for this discrepancy may be that in prior studies, participants were significantly
324	older than our subjects (mean ages ranged from 32 to 56 years old compared to ~22 years
325	old). As ageing influences the decline in vascular structure and function (Xu et al., 2017) and,
326	given that our participants were free from cardiovascular disease risk factors, it is likely that
327	our participants’ vasculature was intact and working optimally, whereas participants in
328	previous studies were possibly experiencing some degree of vascular decline. Taken together,
329	these data suggest that plant-based diets confer protection from, or a slowing of, age-induced
330	vascular degeneration, but do not upregulate an already intact vasculature, however, this
331	hypothesis needs to be explored further. Finally, the assessment of endothelial function by
332	Lin et al (2001) utilises an outdated methodology, which is highly likely to result in
333	inaccuracies in the data collected. Therefore, it remains unclear whether, and in whom, plant-
334	based diets improve vascular outcomes, but it appears that age may be an important factor to
335	consider for future research.
336	Unlike vascular properties, to our knowledge, no previous study has investigated the effects
337	of habitual vegan diet on skeletal muscle architecture. The VL muscle thickness and fascicle
338	pennation angle values in our study were similar to those reported previously in similar
339	populations (Erskine et al., 2011; Erskine et al., 2010; Franchi et al., 2018). We found no
340	differences in VL thickness or fascicle pennation angle between vegans and omnivores,
341	 13
342	 despite omnivores consuming a higher daily protein intake compared with vegans. This is
343	surprising, given plant-based sources of protein, such as wheat and soy, fail to stimulate
344	muscle protein synthesis to the same extent as some animal protein sources (e.g. whey
345	protein) (Gorissen et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2009). However, it has been demonstrated that
346	gains in lean body mass and muscular strength are similar in response to supplementation
347	with either soy or animal protein sources (Messina et al., 2018). Therefore, although the
348	quality of protein might be important for efficient delivery of amino acids to the muscle
349	following resistance exercise (thereby potentially maximising the muscle hypertrophic
350	response in athletes), it may not be so important in non-resistance trained individuals.
351	Furthermore, although vegans consumed less protein than omnivores in our study, they still
352	consumed 0.9 g/kg/d protein, which is within the recommended range for daily protein intake
353	(0.8-2 g/kg/d) (Thomas et al., 2016), thus potentially explaining the similar muscle size and
354	architecture between our vegans and omnivores.
355	As the architecture of a muscle is related to the force it can produce (Aagaard et al., 2001)
356	and given that no differences were observed in muscle architecture in our study, it was not
357	surprising that no difference existed in MVIC force between vegans and omnivores either. No
358	differences in strength or lean body mass have previously been reported in elite athlete
359	vegetarian and omnivorous men and women (Lynch et al., 2016). Similarly, Boutros et al
360	(2020) demonstrated no differences in leg or chest press 1-RM between young, physically
361	active vegan and omnivorous women. It therefore appears that adopting a vegan diet may not
362	be detrimental for skeletal muscle size, architecture or function in both men and women.
363	Recent findings support those from our study, demonstrating no difference in endurance
364	exercise capacity between vegans, lacto-ovovegetarians and omnivores, albeit in male and
365	female runners (Nebl et al., 2019). However, contradictory findings have also recently been
366	published, suggesting that vegans/vegetarians exhibit greater 𝑉̇ O2max values compared with
367	 14
368	 omnivores (Boutros et al., 2020; Lynch et al., 2016). Intriguingly, the 𝑉̇ O2max differences
369	observed by Lynch et al. were only found in female and not male endurance athletes, and
370	only when normalised to body mass. Although not reported, the ratio of lean mass to total
371	body mass appeared to be higher in the female VEG vs. OMN, and a relatively greater
372	skeletal muscle composition would be expected to utilise more O2 during maximal exercise,
373	particularly when normalised to total body mass (which was higher in female OMN vs.VEG).
374	Alternatively, differences in 𝑉̇ O2max could have been caused by the higher weekly energy
375	expenditure in the female VEG vs. OMN (~20 METS, kcal∙kg-1∙week-1), rather than any
376	dietary effect per se. Further, Boutros et al. used a non-validated single question for
377	participants to self-report their physical activity level, while 𝑉̇ O2max was estimated rather than
378	measured directly, both likely having implications for the accuracy of the data (Boutros et al.,
379	2020). It is therefore difficult to discern whether the differences in 𝑉̇ O2max reported in the
380	studies by Lynch et al. and Boutros et al. were due to differences in diet, physical activity, or
381	body composition.
382	While we did not find any effect of diet on 𝑉̇ O2max, vascular or skeletal muscle properties, we
383	did observe between group differences in key micronutrients, which can impact vascular and
384	muscular health. Firstly, our vegans were deficient in vitamin B12 and consumed less than
385	their omnivorous counterparts. However, two vegan participants reported vitamin B12
386	supplementation but did not specify dose/frequency and did not include any relevant
387	information in their food diary, so it could not be included in their dietary analysis. Vitamin
388	B12 deficiency is common amongst vegans (Sobiecki et al., 2016) and can lead to
389	hyperhomocysteinaemia (Krajčovičová-Kudláčková et al., 2000), a condition that is
390	associated with atherosclerosis development (de Koning et al., 2003). However, there was no
391	evidence of altered vasculature in our vegan population, potentially as a result of lower intake
392	of saturated fat and cholesterol and higher vitamin C ingestion than omnivores, which is in
393	 15
394	 accordance with previous findings (Sobiecki et al., 2016). Vitamin C has antioxidant
395	properties and has subsequently been associated with a reduced rate of cIMT growth
396	(Ellingsen et al., 2009) and prevention of endothelial dysfunction (May and Harrison, 2013).
397	Furthermore, vitamin C is also an essential co-factor for lysyl oxidase activation in the
398	collagen synthesis pathway (Boyera et al., 1998), which in turn, could be important for bone,
399	tendon and intramuscular connective tissue health and function. Future studies should
400	investigate whether differences between vegans and omnivores exist regarding other
401	collagenous tissues, such as tendon properties.
402	Limitations and Future Directions
403	Our cohort included young, healthy, recreationally active men in order to minimise the effect
404	of any potential confounders such as ageing (Narici et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2017), training
405	status (Erskine et al., 2010; Green and Smith, 2018; McPhee et al., 2009) or disease incidence
406	(Li et al., 2015; Vrtovec et al., 1999) on vascular and skeletal muscle phenotypes. We also
407	utilised updated vascular assessment protocols (Thijssen et al., 2019) and included
408	measurements of skeletal muscle architecture and isometric strength to draw more precise
409	comparisons between vegan and omnivorous dieters, regarding vascular health and skeletal
410	muscle structure and function. We do acknowledge that additional measures of muscle size,
411	e.g. volume of the four individual heads of the quadriceps femoris muscle group, may have
412	provided more support for our findings. However, we chose to study the VL, because it is the
413	largest of the four quadriceps femoris heads (Erskine et al., 2009) and VL muscle thickness
414	(measured with ultrasound) correlates strongly with muscle volume (measured with MRI),
415	both before and after chronic resistance training (Franchi et al., 2018). Thus, the fact that we
416	found no difference in VL muscle thickness or fascicle pennation angle between VEG and
417	OMN suggests we would not have observed a difference in quadriceps femoris muscle
418	volume either.
419	 16
420	 Regarding the assessment of dietary behaviour, food diaries are a prospective dietary
421	assessment tool that provide detailed descriptions of foods consumed as well as portion sizes
422	and cooking/preparation methods. However, participants may alter both the type and amount
423	of food they consume during the assessment (Rebro et al., 1998). We acknowledge that a
424	longer recording period and/or additional assessments of weighed nutrient intake might have
425	provided a more comprehensive account of habitual diet (Ortega et al., 2015) and further
426	reinforced our results. However, in light of potential participant fatigue (Vereecken et al.,
427	2008) and, with the accuracy of seven-day recording periods decreasing in the later stages
428	(Ortega et al., 2015), a three-day food diary was deemed most appropriate. Furthermore, we
429	did not measure amino acid intake in the current study, which could have provided further
430	information regarding skeletal muscle and vascular health (Churchward‐ Venne et al., 2012;
431	Huynh and Chin‐ Dusting, 2006). For example, leucine is considered the most important
432	amino acid for stimulating muscle protein synthesis (Churchward‐ Venne et al., 2012), and is
433	more abundant in whey compared to soy protein (Tang et al., 2009). However, there are a
434	number of vegan-suitable protein sources that contain all nine EAAs (e.g. soy, quinoa and
435	buckwheat), but it may be that the quantity rather than quality of protein is more important
436	for maintaining muscle health, particularly in non-athletes. Finally, we examined the impact
437	of a vegan diet in a young, healthy cohort in order to remove ageing as a potential
438	confounding variable, however, it is possible that no differences were observed between
439	vegans and omnivores due to the lack of muscular or vascular degeneration that is seen with
440	ageing (Narici et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2017).
441	Conclusion
442	With these results, we show for the first time that young, healthy, recreationally active vegan
443	and omnivorous men do not differ regarding novel measurements of vascular and skeletal
444	muscle structure and function, despite differences in key macro- and micronutrient intake.
445	 17
446	 Our data, therefore, indicate that a healthy vegan diet is neither beneficial nor detrimental for
447	vascular and skeletal muscle health when compared with an omnivorous diet in young,
448	healthy, untrained men.
449	Declarations
450	Disclosure of interest
451	The authors report no conflicts of interests or competing interests
452	Funding
453	No funding was obtained for this study.
454	Ethics approval
455	The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Liverpool John Moores

measurement approach for FMD (Thijssen et al., 2019). More recently, research has
demonstrated lower cIMT in young healthy vegetarian men compared with their omnivorous
counterparts (Acosta-Navarro et al., 2017). To our knowledge there is only one study that has
investigated the effects of a vegan diet on the vasculature, indicating that microvascular
function did not improve following just four weeks compliance to a vegan diet (Rogerson et
al., 2018). Consequently, it is unclear whether a habitual vegan diet confers any direct
benefits to vascular structure or function.
Despite the purported health benefits, there are potential risks of nutrient deficiencies
associated with vegan diets. Protein intake, for example, is lower in vegan dieters compared
with omnivores, and in some cases less than the minimum recommended daily protein intake
(Sobiecki et al., 2016). Protein consumption increases postprandial myofibrillar protein
synthesis (MPS) rates (Tipton et al., 1999), subsequently contributing to muscle mass
accretion (Hartman et al., 2007). Given that muscle mass is the main determinant of
maximum strength (Jones et al., 1989), it is plausible that lower protein consumption in
 4
 vegan diets could be associated with (smaller and therefore) weaker muscles (Sahni et al.,
2015). However, previous studies have demonstrated no differences in upper and lower body
one-repetition maximum (1-RM) (Boutros et al., 2020), or knee extensor isokinetic peak
torque between young physically active vegan/vegetarian and omnivorous women (Lynch et
al., 2016) Nonetheless, as participants were highly trained, it is not clear how training status
and the interaction with diet may have impacted these findings. It should also be noted that
no prior studies have included assessment of muscle morphology or architecture. Skeletal
muscle architecture (including thickness and fascicle pennation angle) are key determinants
of the maximum force of a muscle (Aagaard et al., 2001), therefore assessment of muscle
architecture in habitual, untrained vegan and omnivorous dieters may confirm existing
evidence suggesting similarities in maximal muscle strength.
Despite the potential disadvantages of plant-based diets for strength/power performance,
evidence suggests no differences exist in maximal power output during an incremental
cycling bout between vegans, lacto-ovovegetarians and omnivores (Nebl et al., 2019).
Contrarily, there is some evidence that 𝑉̇ O2max is higher in female elite vegetarian vs.
omnivore endurance athletes (Lynch et al., 2016). Further, highly physically active (150-200
minutes of moderate intensity physical activity/week) vegan females exhibit a greater
estimated 𝑉̇ O2max when compared with omnivores (Boutros et al., 2020). However,
estimating rather than measuring 𝑉̇ O2max is problematic and both studies used highly trained
populations, which limits the application of the study findings. For example, chronic
endurance (McPhee et al., 2009) and resistance (Erskine et al., 2011; Erskine et al., 2010)
exercise, as well as ageing (Janssen et al., 2000) induce physiological adaptations that will
likely confound any measurable effect of diet on vascular or muscle properties.
To date, no study has combined ultrasound assessments of vascular structure and function
with skeletal muscle architecture, as well as maximal force and measured 𝑉̇ O2max, in habitual
 5
 vegan and omnivorous dieters. The aim of this study, therefore, was to compare the vascular
and skeletal muscle properties between young, healthy, untrained men who were either
habitual vegan or omnivorous dieters. We hypothesised that vegan dieters would have higher
FMD and 𝑉̇ O2max, but lower cIMT values compared with omnivorous dieters, whereas
omnivores would have larger and stronger knee extensor muscles.
Methods
Twenty-five young, healthy men with no history of resistance or endurance exercise training
in the preceding six months were recruited for the current study, which was a single-centre,
cross-sectional design. Participant characteristics are shown in Table 1. Further exclusion
criteria included smokers, those with a history of lower limb injuries in the six months prior
to testing and those engaging in more than two hours per week of structured exercise.
Participants were established as vegans or omnivores via a series of questions regarding
consumption of meat, fish/seafood, eggs and dairy products such as milk and cheese.
Subsequently, vegans were defined as those who consumed no animal products in their diet
for at least six months prior to testing, and omnivores were defined as those who consumed
animal products (including meat) in their habitual diet. This was then confirmed following
completion of a three-day food diary (see below). Sixteen omnivores (OMN) and nine vegans
(VEG) provided written informed consent prior to taking part in the study, which was
approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Liverpool John Moores University (approval
number: U18SPS007) and complied with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical
Association, 2013).
Experimental design. All participants visited the laboratory on three occasions and were
instructed to abstain from alcohol (at least 24 h before each visit) and caffeine consumption
the day of each visit. Additionally, the participants underwent an overnight fast and avoided
exercise for 24 hours prior to the first visit. During the first visit, a brachial artery FMD and
 6
 cIMT assessment was conducted by the same trained sonographer for all trials. Following the
vascular assessment, participants were familiarised with the protocol for the knee extension
maximum voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) assessment in the right leg on the
isokinetic dynamometer (IKD), and the 𝑉̇ O2max test on a cycle ergometer, for which they
completed the warm-up and first stage only. Participants were then provided with a three-day
food diary and received full instructions on how to complete the diary. During visit two,
subjects underwent an assessment of vastus lateralis (VL) muscle architecture using
ultrasonography and completed a quadriceps MVIC on the IKD. The final visit occurred at
least two days following visit two and incorporated a 𝑉̇ O2max test to volitional fatigue on a
cycle ergometer.
Vascular Assessment. Participants arrived at the laboratory at 08.00 hours. They then lay in
the supine position for 20 min before extending their right arm at an approximate 80° angle
from the torso. All ultrasound measures were carried out by the same trained sonographer
using high-resolution ultrasonography (Acuson, Terason, t3000, Teratec, USA) with a 40 mm
wide 10-12 MHz probe.
FMD was assessed in the brachial artery in the distal third of the upper arm at an angle of
60°. Ultrasound parameters remained constant throughout each assessment, with the probe
held in a constant position, to optimize longitudinal two-dimensional B mode images of the
near arterial wall. A 1 min baseline measurement of artery diameter was recorded prior to a
rapid inflator (AG 101 Hokanson, Bellevue, USA) inflating the forearm cuff to 220 mmHg
for a 5 min ischaemic stimulus. The endothelium-mediated vasodilation response to the cuff
deflation was then recorded, beginning 30 s prior to deflation, for a period of 3 min,
according to previous guidelines (Thijssen et al., 2019). Post-test analysis was performed
using custom designed automated edge detection and wall tracking software. B mode images
were analysed at ~20 Hz, with a specific region of interest identified and lumen diameter then
 7
 calculated by averaging the number of pixel columns in each frame. Shear rate (SR) was then
calculated as the area under the curve (AUC) up to maximal post-deflation diameter. The
test-retest coefficient of variation (CV) for FMD measurements previously performed in our
laboratory is 11.7% (Carter et al., 2019), which is within the acceptable limits of 15%
(Thijssen et al., 2019).
For cIMT assessment, participants remained in the supine position, with the head tilted 90° to
the left. The common carotid artery was examined ~1 cm proximal to the bulbus and
ultrasound parameters set to optimize longitudinal two-dimensional B mode images of the
luminal-wall interface. The probe and ultrasound parameters were held constant throughout
each scan. Once a clear image with visible contrast between the arterial lumen, walls and
IMT was established a 30 s video was recorded at approximately 40°, 90° and 150° angles.
All assessments were carried out by the same researcher. Post-test analysis was performed
using v3.0 custom designed edge detection software with the most distinct 6-8 s from
recorded scans containing an optimal area of 1 cm including both vessel walls selected for
analysis. The software produced an edge detection output from the lumen-intima interface
and the media-adventitia interface at each angle to provide an average IMT and lumen
diameter over the 6-8 s. The mean cIMT and diameter calculated from the 3 recorded angles
is presented. The test-retest CVs for carotid artery wall thickness and diameter measurements
previously recorded in our laboratory are 8.6% and 3.6%, respectively (Hopkins et al., 2013).
VL Muscle Architecture. Participants were seated in an IKD chair (Lido Active, Loredan,
Davis, CA, USA), with a hip angle of 90° (180° = supine) and a 90° knee flexion angle (0° =
full knee extension). The length of the VL was determined at rest by measuring the distance
between the muscle origin and insertion, identified via B-mode ultrasonography (40 mm/10-
15 MHz transducer, MyLab30, Esaote, Genoa, Italy). The medial and lateral borders of the
VL were determined at 50% of the muscle length to establish the middle of the muscle belly
 8
 for the assessment. Two sagittal ultrasound images were taken at this site with the probe
placed perpendicular to the skin, in line with the muscle fascicles. Depth and frequency were
altered to obtain the optimal image, with both deep and superficial aponeuroses and at least
three fascicles clearly visible. Subsequently, images were analysed using a computer software
package (NIH ImageJ, version 1.39b, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, USA). Muscle
thickness was measured using the mean value from three measurements of the distance
between the superficial and deep aponeuroses, while fascicle pennation angle was measured
using the mean value of three fascicles inserting into the deep aponeurosis. The test-retest
CVs for VL muscle thickness and fascicle pennation angle measurements in this study were
4.9% and 5.8%, respectively.
Knee Extension MVIC. Participants remained seated in the IKD as above. They were securely
strapped with inextensible straps around the waist and chest to prevent movement, and the
right ankle was strapped to the force transducer (KAP, Bienfait B.V. Haarlem, The
Netherlands). Force output was recorded using a data acquisition package (Acqknowledge,
Biopac Systems, CA, USA). Ten submaximal contractions were completed as a warm-up
with participants increasing their force output each time. Once fully prepared, participants
were instructed to perform two MVICs separated by a one-minute rest period. The true
MVIC value was determined by a difference of < 5 % between each trial, with trials being
repeated if larger differences occurred. Verbal encouragement was provided by researchers
and feedback was provided to participants by projecting their MVIC attempts on a screen in
front of them in real time. Test-retest CV for the MVIC measurement in this study was 4.5%.
𝑉̇ O2max. During the final visit participants completed a 𝑉̇ O2max test to volitional fatigue on a
cycle ergometer (Lode Corival, Groningen, Netherlands). Upon arrival at the laboratory
participants rested for ten minutes before their resting heart rate was measured (Polar,
Kempele, Finland) and their blood lactate measurement (Nova Biomedical, Massachusetts,
 9
 USA) was taken from a finger prick blood sample. The participant was fitted with a facemask
to collect inspired and expired air. The test began with a 3 min warm up cycling at a power
output of 50 W, before the first stage started with subjects cycling at 95 W. The power output
increased by 35 W every 3 min until volitional fatigue, with heart rate (HR), blood lactate and
rate of perceived exertion (RPE via Borg Scale) recorded at the end of each increment.
Expired air samples were measured using an online gas analysis system (Cortex, Leipzig,
Germany) to determine 𝑉̇ O2 and respiratory exchange ratio (RER). The criteria to determine
whether 𝑉̇ O2max had been reached consisted of a HR value within 10 bpm of subjects’ age-
predicted HR maximum (220-minus age in years), a blood lactate value > 8.0 mmol.L-1, an
RER > 1.15 and if subjects were unable to maintain the optimum cycling cadence of 80 rpm.
Final HR, blood lactate, RER and RPE measurements were taken immediately following
cessation of the test. Test-retest CV for 𝑉̇ O2max assessment in this study was 5.2%.
Dietary Analysis. Participants were provided with a three-day food diary with full
instructions to record all food and drink consumed over two weekdays (Thursday and Friday)
and one weekend day (Saturday). A three-day food diary was deemed appropriate, as
opposed to the seven-day method that has previously been suggested to decrease in validity in
the later days, due to participant fatigue and foods being recorded retrospectively (Thompson
and Subar, 2017). Time of consumption and quantity of food were also recorded. Dietary
diary analysis was conducted using an online dietary analysis software (Nutritics, Research
Edition (v5.5), Dublin, Ireland), which produced a full dietary report (including macro and
micronutrients). In a separate questionnaire, participants were asked if they consumed any
dietary supplements and, if so, what dose/frequency. Just two (both vegans) reported taking
vitamin B12 (one participant) and omega-3 and vitamin B12 (one participant), although
dose/frequency were not stated. Further, these participants did not record consumption of
these supplements in their food diary, so they were not included in their dietary analysis.
 10
 Statistical Analysis. Differences between groups were estimated via a Bayesian analysis of
independent groups, comprising a null hypothesis (H0 = there are no differences between
OMN and VEG for each outcome variable measured) and an alternative hypothesis (H1 =
differences exist between OMN and VEG for each outcome variable measured).
Uninformative priors were assumed for all statistical analyses and statistical outputs are
presented as estimated mean differences (EMD), with 95% credible intervals (CI) and Bayes
factors (BF). Data for BF are presented as BF01 (null hypothesis given alternative hypothesis)
and can be interpreted as evidence to support the hypotheses based on previously defined
thresholds- BF01 = 1-3 and 3-10 represent anecdotal and moderate strength evidence for H0,
respectively (Lee and Wagenmakers, 2013). Whereas a BF01 = 0.1-0.33, 0.033-0.1 and 0.01-
0.033 represent moderate, strong and very strong evidence for H1, respectively (Lee and
Wagenmakers, 2013). All statistical analyses were performed with SPSS 26 (IBM SPSS
Statistics for Windows, Version 26.0. Armonk, New York, USA) and data are presented as
means ± SD.
Results
Participant physical characteristics are displayed in Table 1. There was ‘strong’ evidence to
suggest VEG were older than OMN (BF01 = 0.043).

Daily nutrient intake (both in absolute terms and normalised to body mass) are presented in
Table 2. Compared to OMN, there was ‘moderate’ to ‘extremely strong’ evidence to suggest
VEG ingested less protein, saturated fat, cholesterol and vitamin B12, but more fibre, iron and
vitamin C (BF01 = 0.259 - 0.000).

 11
 Vascular data are presented in Table 3. Due to technical issues, cIMT data were excluded
from one OMN and one VEG, and FMD data from two OMN. There was ‘anecdotal’
evidence to suggest vascular properties did not differ between VEG and OMN (BF01 = 1.557
- 2.591).

The estimated mean difference (EMD) in muscle thickness between OMN and VEG was -
1.72 mm (95% CI = -6.33 to 2.89, BF01 = 2.726, Fig 1A) and for fascicle pennation angle was
-1.09° (95% CI = -5.52 to 3.35, BF01 = 2.844, Fig 1B). Furthermore, the EMD in both
absolute and relative MVIC values were 75.93 N (95% CI = -85.27 to 237.13, BF01 = 1.656,
Fig 1C) and 1.214 N/kg (CI = -1.262 to 3.689, BF01 = 1.470, Fig 1D), respectively, indicating
no differences in muscle properties between OMN and VEG. The EMD in absolute and
relative 𝑉̇ O2max between OMN and VEG were 0.24 L/min (95% CI = -0.39 to 0.87, BF01 =
2.392, Fig 1E) and 4.81 mL/kg/min (95% CI = -3.77 to 13.40, BF01 = 1.218, Fig 1F),
respectively, therefore indicating no differences between groups.
