Discussion
This is the first study to combine ultrasound assessments of vascular and skeletal muscle
properties, as well as maximal muscle force and 𝑉̇ O2max, for comparison between healthy,
young, untrained habitual vegan and omnivorous men. Importantly, by assessing young,
recreationally active but non-resistance/endurance trained individuals, we were able to
examine the effect of a vegan diet on the vasculature and musculature independent of training
status and ageing. Our novel findings demonstrate that no differences existed in vascular
structure and function, or skeletal muscle properties, between habitual vegan and omnivorous
 12
 dieters despite marked differences in macro- and micronutrient intake. Additionally, vegans
and omnivores did not differ regarding cardiorespiratory fitness.
Prior research has demonstrated both higher FMD scores and smaller cIMT values in
vegetarians compared with omnivores (Acosta-Navarro et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2001).
However, in our study, we demonstrate in a young, recreationally active male cohort that
there were no differences in vascular structure or function between vegans and omnivores,
despite vegans consuming less saturated fat and cholesterol in their diet. One possible
explanation for this discrepancy may be that in prior studies, participants were significantly
older than our subjects (mean ages ranged from 32 to 56 years old compared to ~22 years
old). As ageing influences the decline in vascular structure and function (Xu et al., 2017) and,
given that our participants were free from cardiovascular disease risk factors, it is likely that
our participants’ vasculature was intact and working optimally, whereas participants in
previous studies were possibly experiencing some degree of vascular decline. Taken together,
these data suggest that plant-based diets confer protection from, or a slowing of, age-induced
vascular degeneration, but do not upregulate an already intact vasculature, however, this
hypothesis needs to be explored further. Finally, the assessment of endothelial function by
Lin et al (2001) utilises an outdated methodology, which is highly likely to result in
inaccuracies in the data collected. Therefore, it remains unclear whether, and in whom, plant-
based diets improve vascular outcomes, but it appears that age may be an important factor to
consider for future research.
Unlike vascular properties, to our knowledge, no previous study has investigated the effects
of habitual vegan diet on skeletal muscle architecture. The VL muscle thickness and fascicle
pennation angle values in our study were similar to those reported previously in similar
populations (Erskine et al., 2011; Erskine et al., 2010; Franchi et al., 2018). We found no
differences in VL thickness or fascicle pennation angle between vegans and omnivores,
 13
 despite omnivores consuming a higher daily protein intake compared with vegans. This is
surprising, given plant-based sources of protein, such as wheat and soy, fail to stimulate
muscle protein synthesis to the same extent as some animal protein sources (e.g. whey
protein) (Gorissen et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2009). However, it has been demonstrated that
gains in lean body mass and muscular strength are similar in response to supplementation
with either soy or animal protein sources (Messina et al., 2018). Therefore, although the
quality of protein might be important for efficient delivery of amino acids to the muscle
following resistance exercise (thereby potentially maximising the muscle hypertrophic
response in athletes), it may not be so important in non-resistance trained individuals.
Furthermore, although vegans consumed less protein than omnivores in our study, they still
consumed 0.9 g/kg/d protein, which is within the recommended range for daily protein intake
(0.8-2 g/kg/d) (Thomas et al., 2016), thus potentially explaining the similar muscle size and
architecture between our vegans and omnivores.
As the architecture of a muscle is related to the force it can produce (Aagaard et al., 2001)
and given that no differences were observed in muscle architecture in our study, it was not
surprising that no difference existed in MVIC force between vegans and omnivores either. No
differences in strength or lean body mass have previously been reported in elite athlete
vegetarian and omnivorous men and women (Lynch et al., 2016). Similarly, Boutros et al
(2020) demonstrated no differences in leg or chest press 1-RM between young, physically
active vegan and omnivorous women. It therefore appears that adopting a vegan diet may not
be detrimental for skeletal muscle size, architecture or function in both men and women.
Recent findings support those from our study, demonstrating no difference in endurance
exercise capacity between vegans, lacto-ovovegetarians and omnivores, albeit in male and
female runners (Nebl et al., 2019). However, contradictory findings have also recently been
published, suggesting that vegans/vegetarians exhibit greater 𝑉̇ O2max values compared with
 14
 omnivores (Boutros et al., 2020; Lynch et al., 2016). Intriguingly, the 𝑉̇ O2max differences
observed by Lynch et al. were only found in female and not male endurance athletes, and
only when normalised to body mass. Although not reported, the ratio of lean mass to total
body mass appeared to be higher in the female VEG vs. OMN, and a relatively greater
skeletal muscle composition would be expected to utilise more O2 during maximal exercise,
particularly when normalised to total body mass (which was higher in female OMN vs.VEG).
Alternatively, differences in 𝑉̇ O2max could have been caused by the higher weekly energy
expenditure in the female VEG vs. OMN (~20 METS, kcal∙kg-1∙week-1), rather than any
dietary effect per se. Further, Boutros et al. used a non-validated single question for
participants to self-report their physical activity level, while 𝑉̇ O2max was estimated rather than
measured directly, both likely having implications for the accuracy of the data (Boutros et al.,
2020). It is therefore difficult to discern whether the differences in 𝑉̇ O2max reported in the
studies by Lynch et al. and Boutros et al. were due to differences in diet, physical activity, or
body composition.
While we did not find any effect of diet on 𝑉̇ O2max, vascular or skeletal muscle properties, we
did observe between group differences in key micronutrients, which can impact vascular and
muscular health. Firstly, our vegans were deficient in vitamin B12 and consumed less than
their omnivorous counterparts. However, two vegan participants reported vitamin B12
supplementation but did not specify dose/frequency and did not include any relevant
information in their food diary, so it could not be included in their dietary analysis. Vitamin
B12 deficiency is common amongst vegans (Sobiecki et al., 2016) and can lead to
hyperhomocysteinaemia (Krajčovičová-Kudláčková et al., 2000), a condition that is
associated with atherosclerosis development (de Koning et al., 2003). However, there was no
evidence of altered vasculature in our vegan population, potentially as a result of lower intake
of saturated fat and cholesterol and higher vitamin C ingestion than omnivores, which is in
 15
 accordance with previous findings (Sobiecki et al., 2016). Vitamin C has antioxidant
properties and has subsequently been associated with a reduced rate of cIMT growth
(Ellingsen et al., 2009) and prevention of endothelial dysfunction (May and Harrison, 2013).
Furthermore, vitamin C is also an essential co-factor for lysyl oxidase activation in the
collagen synthesis pathway (Boyera et al., 1998), which in turn, could be important for bone,
tendon and intramuscular connective tissue health and function. Future studies should
investigate whether differences between vegans and omnivores exist regarding other
collagenous tissues, such as tendon properties.
Limitations and Future Directions
Our cohort included young, healthy, recreationally active men in order to minimise the effect
of any potential confounders such as ageing (Narici et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2017), training
status (Erskine et al., 2010; Green and Smith, 2018; McPhee et al., 2009) or disease incidence
(Li et al., 2015; Vrtovec et al., 1999) on vascular and skeletal muscle phenotypes. We also
utilised updated vascular assessment protocols (Thijssen et al., 2019) and included
measurements of skeletal muscle architecture and isometric strength to draw more precise
comparisons between vegan and omnivorous dieters, regarding vascular health and skeletal
muscle structure and function. We do acknowledge that additional measures of muscle size,
e.g. volume of the four individual heads of the quadriceps femoris muscle group, may have
provided more support for our findings. However, we chose to study the VL, because it is the
largest of the four quadriceps femoris heads (Erskine et al., 2009) and VL muscle thickness
(measured with ultrasound) correlates strongly with muscle volume (measured with MRI),
both before and after chronic resistance training (Franchi et al., 2018). Thus, the fact that we
found no difference in VL muscle thickness or fascicle pennation angle between VEG and
OMN suggests we would not have observed a difference in quadriceps femoris muscle
volume either.
 16
 Regarding the assessment of dietary behaviour, food diaries are a prospective dietary
assessment tool that provide detailed descriptions of foods consumed as well as portion sizes
and cooking/preparation methods. However, participants may alter both the type and amount
of food they consume during the assessment (Rebro et al., 1998). We acknowledge that a
longer recording period and/or additional assessments of weighed nutrient intake might have
provided a more comprehensive account of habitual diet (Ortega et al., 2015) and further
reinforced our results. However, in light of potential participant fatigue (Vereecken et al.,
2008) and, with the accuracy of seven-day recording periods decreasing in the later stages
(Ortega et al., 2015), a three-day food diary was deemed most appropriate. Furthermore, we
did not measure amino acid intake in the current study, which could have provided further
information regarding skeletal muscle and vascular health (Churchward‐ Venne et al., 2012;
Huynh and Chin‐ Dusting, 2006). For example, leucine is considered the most important
amino acid for stimulating muscle protein synthesis (Churchward‐ Venne et al., 2012), and is
more abundant in whey compared to soy protein (Tang et al., 2009). However, there are a
number of vegan-suitable protein sources that contain all nine EAAs (e.g. soy, quinoa and
buckwheat), but it may be that the quantity rather than quality of protein is more important
for maintaining muscle health, particularly in non-athletes. Finally, we examined the impact
of a vegan diet in a young, healthy cohort in order to remove ageing as a potential
confounding variable, however, it is possible that no differences were observed between
vegans and omnivores due to the lack of muscular or vascular degeneration that is seen with
ageing (Narici et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2017).
Conclusion
With these results, we show for the first time that young, healthy, recreationally active vegan
and omnivorous men do not differ regarding novel measurements of vascular and skeletal
muscle structure and function, despite differences in key macro- and micronutrient intake.
 17
 Our data, therefore, indicate that a healthy vegan diet is neither beneficial nor detrimental for
vascular and skeletal muscle health when compared with an omnivorous diet in young,
healthy, untrained men.
Declarations
Disclosure of interest
The authors report no conflicts of interests or competing interests
Funding
No funding was obtained for this study.
Ethics approval
The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Liverpool John Moores

{
 "id": "Q54",
 "sourceFile": "Skimmed, lactose-free milk ingestion postexercise - Rehydration effectiveness and gastrointestinal disturbances vs water and a sports drink in physically active people.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'Skimmed, Lactose-Free Milk Ingestion Postexercise: Rehydration Effectiveness and Gastrointestinal Disturbances Versus Water and a Sports Drink in Physically Active People' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration"],
 "audiences": ["Nutrition", "Performance", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomized crossover study in which 16 physically active college students (4 women, 12 men) lost about 2% of body mass cycling in a heat chamber at 32 degrees C, then drank 150% of the loss over 90 minutes of water, a sports drink or skimmed lactose-free milk, with follow-up for 3 hours. Fluid retention was about 70% with milk and 40% with water (p < .001), with the sports drink at about 56%, not significantly different from either; mild gastrointestinal symptoms did not differ among drinks.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The sample was 16 physically active students rather than athletes, tested once per drink after a single 2% dehydration, with 3 hours of follow-up. Milk did not differ significantly from the sports drink on fluid retention, and the research was funded by a milk producers' cooperative, which staff should weigh.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read milk as superior to sports drinks for rehydration, but milk outperformed water, while milk and the sports drink did not differ significantly.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Aragón-Vargas LF, Garzón-Mosquera JC, Montoya-Arroyo JA. Skimmed, lactose-free milk ingestion postexercise: rehydration effectiveness and gastrointestinal disturbances versus water and a sports drink in physically active people. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2024.",
  "doi": "10.1123/ijsnem.2023-0253",
  "abstract": "This study compared rehydration after moderate-intensity cycling in the heat with water, a sports drink or skimmed lactose-free milk in 16 physically active college students, measuring net fluid balance, diuresis and gastrointestinal symptoms over 3 hours. Milk showed higher fluid retention (about 69%) than water (about 40%), and the sports drink (about 56%) did not differ from either. Gastrointestinal symptoms were mild and did not differ among drinks.",
  "tldr": "After a 2% body-mass loss in heat, skimmed lactose-free milk retained more fluid than water over 3 hours, with mild gut symptoms similar to the other drinks. It was not significantly different from a sports drink on fluid retention.",
  "methods": "Randomized crossover design in which 16 physically active college students each completed three sessions of cycling in a heat chamber (32 degrees C, 70% relative humidity) to lose about 2% of body mass. They then drank 150% of the loss in three aliquots over 90 minutes, with water, a sports drink or skimmed lactose-free milk, and fluid balance, urine output and gastrointestinal symptoms were measured for 3 hours.",
  "findings": "Fluid retention was about 69.8% for milk, 55.6% for the sports drink and 39.6% for water. Net fluid balance at 3 hours was -0.26 kg for milk, -0.42 kg for the sports drink and -0.67 kg for water. Both milk (-0.40 kg) and the sports drink (-0.25 kg) differed significantly from water, while milk and the sports drink did not differ (-0.15 kg, p = .126). Gastrointestinal symptom scores were low and did not differ among conditions.",
  "limitations": "The sample was small and recreationally active rather than trained athletes, and only one heat exposure with about 2 L of fluid was tested. The milk versus sports drink difference was not significant for fluid retention or net fluid balance, so the ranking of those two drinks is not established. The milk and sports drink also differed in protein, carbohydrate, fat and potassium, so the study cannot say which component drives retention.",
  "practicalImplications": "After a moderate sweat loss in heat, skimmed lactose-free milk may be a practical rehydration option if it is tolerated, since it retained more fluid than water. The sports drink was not significantly different from milk, so choice can rest on tolerance and preference.",
  "athleteDev": "For athletes rehydrating after training in the heat, milk gave better fluid retention than water in this study, so it is a reasonable option if the athlete tolerates it. The study did not test carbohydrate or electrolyte goals, so it does not settle drink choice for performance needs.",
  "rtp": "Cannot inform return to sport: the participants were physically active students without injury, and the study measured only post-exercise hydration."
 }
}

1	International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism, (Ahead of Print)
2	https://doi.org/10.1123/ijsnem.2023-0253 ORIGINAL RESEARCH
3	First Published Online: May 24, 2024
4	 Skimmed, Lactose-Free Milk Ingestion Postexercise: Rehydration
5	 Effectiveness and Gastrointestinal Disturbances Versus Water
6	 and a Sports Drink in Physically Active People
7	 Luis F. Aragón-Vargas, Julián C. Garzón-Mosquera, and Johnny A. Montoya-Arroyo
8	 Human Movement Science Research Center (CIMOHU-UCR), University of Costa Rica (UCR), San Jose, Costa Rica
9	 Postexercise hydration is fundamental to replace ﬂuid loss from sweat. This study evaluated rehydration and gastrointestinal (GI)
10	 symptoms for each of three beverages: water (W), sports drink (SD), and skimmed, lactose-free milk (SLM) after moderate-
11	 intensity cycling in the heat. Sixteen college students completed three exercise sessions each to lose ≈2% of their body mass.
12	 They drank 150% of body mass loss of the drink assigned in randomized order; net ﬂuid balance, diuresis, and GI symptoms were
13	 measured and followed up for 3 hr after completion of ﬂuid intake. SLM showed higher ﬂuid retention (∼69%) versus W (∼40%;
14	 p < .001); SD (∼56%) was not different from SLM or W (p > .05). Net ﬂuid balance was higher for SLM (−0.26 kg) and SD
15	 (−0.42 kg) than W (−0.67 kg) after 3 hr (p < .001), resulting from a signiﬁcantly lower diuresis with SLM. Reported GI
16	 disturbances were mild and showed no difference among drinks (p > .05) despite ingestion of W (1,992 ± 425 ml), SD
17	 (1,999 ± 429 ml), and SLM (1,993 ± 426 ml) in 90 min. In conclusion, SLM was more effective than W for postexercise
18	 rehydration, showing greater ﬂuid retention for the 3-hr follow-up and presenting with low-intensity GI symptoms similar to
19	 those with W and SD. These results conﬁrm that SLM is an effective option for hydration after exercise in the heat.
20	 Keywords: hydration, acute GI problems, ﬂuid balance, dairy
21	 Dehydration during prolonged exercise in the heat is a com- effectiveness of 13 beverages by calculating a beverage hydration
22	mon occurrence requiring ﬂuid and electrolyte ingestion to main- index (BHI), using a reference value for W = 1.00. After correction
23	tain homeostasis and prevent muscle fatigue, cramping, and heat for the W content of each beverage, oral rehydration solutions
24	exhaustion (Sawka et al., 2007). Postexercise rehydration involves obtained a mean BHI of 1.50 (p = .01), while skimmed milk

 Skimmed, Lactose-Free Milk Ingestion Postexercise: Rehydration
 Effectiveness and Gastrointestinal Disturbances Versus Water
 and a Sports Drink in Physically Active People
 Luis F. Aragón-Vargas, Julián C. Garzón-Mosquera, and Johnny A. Montoya-Arroyo
 Human Movement Science Research Center (CIMOHU-UCR), University of Costa Rica (UCR), San Jose, Costa Rica
 Postexercise hydration is fundamental to replace ﬂuid loss from sweat. This study evaluated rehydration and gastrointestinal (GI)
 symptoms for each of three beverages: water (W), sports drink (SD), and skimmed, lactose-free milk (SLM) after moderate-
 intensity cycling in the heat. Sixteen college students completed three exercise sessions each to lose ≈2% of their body mass.
 They drank 150% of body mass loss of the drink assigned in randomized order; net ﬂuid balance, diuresis, and GI symptoms were
 measured and followed up for 3 hr after completion of ﬂuid intake. SLM showed higher ﬂuid retention (∼69%) versus W (∼40%;
 p < .001); SD (∼56%) was not different from SLM or W (p > .05). Net ﬂuid balance was higher for SLM (−0.26 kg) and SD
 (−0.42 kg) than W (−0.67 kg) after 3 hr (p < .001), resulting from a signiﬁcantly lower diuresis with SLM. Reported GI
 disturbances were mild and showed no difference among drinks (p > .05) despite ingestion of W (1,992 ± 425 ml), SD
 (1,999 ± 429 ml), and SLM (1,993 ± 426 ml) in 90 min. In conclusion, SLM was more effective than W for postexercise
 rehydration, showing greater ﬂuid retention for the 3-hr follow-up and presenting with low-intensity GI symptoms similar to
 those with W and SD. These results conﬁrm that SLM is an effective option for hydration after exercise in the heat.

p['athleteDev']="In physically active adults rehydrating after exercise in the heat, milk gave better fluid retention than water, so it is a reasonable option for athletes who tolerate it. {
 "id": "Q55",
 "sourceFile": "Skin Tattoos Alter Sweat Rate and        Na+ Concentration.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'Skin Tattoos Alter Sweat Rate and Na+ Concentration' (Luetkemeier, Hanisko, Aho, Med Sci Sports Exerc 2017) matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "low",
 "studyDesign": "Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Within-person laboratory study of 10 apparently healthy young men, each with a tattoo covering at least 5.2 cm2 on one side of the body and untattooed skin on the other. Sweat was induced at rest by pilocarpine iontophoresis, with sweat rate and sweat sodium measured from each site. Sweat rate was about half as high from tattooed skin (0.18 vs 0.35 mg/cm2/min, p = 0.001), and sweat Na+ was higher (69.1 vs 42.6 mmol/L, p = 0.02), with nine of ten men showing the higher sodium on the tattooed side.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Ten healthy non-athlete men were tested at rest with no exercise or heat load, so the study cannot show effects on heat tolerance or hydration during training. The authors call the findings preliminary, the mechanism is unknown, and the link to athletes is background rather than tested.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as proof that tattooed athletes sweat less and lose more sodium in training heat, but the study used resting pilocarpine stimulation with no heat or exercise, so it cannot support any change to hydration or heat plans.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2017,
  "citation": "Luetkemeier MJ, Hanisko JM, Aho KM. Skin tattoos alter sweat rate and Na+ concentration. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2017;49(7):1432-1436.",
  "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000001244",
  "abstract": "The study compared sweat rate and sweat Na+ concentration from tattooed and nontattooed skin in 10 healthy men, using pilocarpine iontophoresis. Tattooed skin produced less sweat (0.18 vs 0.35 mg/cm2/min) and sweat with more sodium (69.1 vs 42.6 mmol/L) than nontattooed skin. The authors conclude that tattooed skin altered sweat function, and the changes did not relate to tattoo age.",
  "tldr": "Tattooed skin sweated about half as much as untattooed skin and gave sweat with higher sodium when stimulated at rest. Whether this changes sweat loss or heat tolerance during exercise has not been tested.",
  "methods": "Within-person comparison in 10 apparently healthy men with a tattoo of at least 5.2 cm2 on one side of the body and untattooed skin at the contralateral site. Sweat was stimulated by two 5-minute cycles of pilocarpine iontophoresis, collected for 20 minutes on a sweat collection disk, and analyzed for rate (by weight) and sodium (by flame photometry). Tattooed and nontattooed sites were compared with paired t-tests, and tattoo age was correlated with the ratios.",
  "findings": "Sweat rate from tattooed skin was 0.18 +/- 0.15 vs 0.35 +/- 0.25 mg/cm2/min for nontattooed skin (p = 0.001), with all 10 men sweating less on the tattooed side (ratio 0.53). Sweat Na+ was 69.1 +/- 28.9 vs 42.6 +/- 15.2 mmol/L (p = 0.02), with nine of ten men higher on the tattooed side. Tattoo age explained less than 1% of the variance in the sweat rate ratio and about 6% of the sodium ratio.",
  "limitations": "The sample was 10 men, the stimulus was pilocarpine at rest in a room controlled at 19 to 21 C, and no heat load or exercise was applied. The authors state the mechanism is unclear, that the results are preliminary, and that it is unknown whether similar changes occur with heat stress or internal heat production.",
  "practicalImplications": "Under pilocarpine stimulation at rest, tattooed skin produced less sweat with a higher sodium concentration, so heavily tattooed athletes may warrant attention in hot conditions. This has not been tested during exercise or heat stress, so it should not change current hydration plans yet.",
  "athleteDev": "This study does not give a performance or training prescription. It suggests tattooed skin may sweat differently, which could matter for heat-training planning, but that needs testing during exercise before it informs practice.",
  "rtp": "Cannot inform return to sport: participants were healthy non-athletes with no injury, and the study measured sweat function at rest only."
 }
}
